Back of the right heel pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Dennis is a new patient training for a triathlon 5 days a week (running ~10k in the mornings, biking 45-60 minutes at lunchtime, and swimming 30-60 minutes in the evening), with long runs or bikes on weekends and one rest day. He does not stretch before workouts. He presents with pain in the back of his right heel, extending up into his calf. The pain occurs typically after a workout, when first getting up in the morning (feels tight and tearing, eases after walking 10-15 minutes), and after sitting for an extended period. Pain is mainly on the right side. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Lower extremities: Right leg affected, left leg is fine.
- Ankle dorsiflexion (pulling toes up): Creates a little bit of pain.
- Resisted plantarflexion (pushing against doctor): Hurts a little bit.
- Thompson test: Negative (squeezing left and right calves produced no pain on either side).
- Right heel/Achilles: Squeezing the right heel causes significant pain. Palpation moving up the Achilles tendon is very tender.

Not discussed.

- Diagnosis: Achilles tendinitis due to overuse from aggressive triathlon training.
- Plan:
  - Stop training for 1 to 2 weeks to allow healing.
  - Medication: Ibuprofen (Advil) 3 tablets every six hours as an anti-inflammatory.
  - Physical therapy: Ordered a couple of visits for strength, stretching understanding, and learning how to stretch muscles before activities.
  - Follow-up: Return in 7 to 10 days following the first couple of physical therapy appointments to monitor progress. If significant pain continues without change after 10 days of activity modification, more aggressive treatment plans may be considered.
  - X-ray: Not indicated at this time.

Not discussed.

Respiratory: No breathing difficulty or respiratory symptoms.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for adult hydrocephalus status post shunt surgery.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
86-year-old male with a history of adult hydrocephalus who returns in follow-up for his first visit since undergoing shunt surgery on August 1st, 2020. He was initially diagnosed with adult hydrocephalus in June 2020 presenting with progressive gait impairment, cognitive impairment, and decreased bladder control. A Medtronic Strata programmable shunt in the ventricular peritoneal configuration was placed, programmed at a level 2.0. Since surgery three months ago, the patient and his daughter report that his walking has improved (now able to walk to the dining room just fine, though still needs help at times). His bladder control improved some after surgery but has leveled out, and he is wearing diapers. Cognition has improved; he does not feel lost when talking to someone anymore, and his daughter notes she feels like she can have a normal conversation with him again. He denies headaches, pain where the shunt is, or belly pain. He has not been hospitalized since surgery. He is asking about driving again; the doctor notes it is unlikely his movement speed will improve to the level needed for a driver safety evaluation at this point, but it could be possible over a 9 to 12 month range if he continues to improve, or he can enroll in a driver safety program preemptively.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional is significant for impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss. GU is significant for urinary incontinence and wearing a diaper. Negative for genital sores, decreased, or painful output. Neurological is significant for continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, or hallucinations. Psychiatric is negative for depression, excessive worrying, or mood swings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 124/80, heart rate 64, respirations 18, weight 174 pounds, pain 0/10.
General: Pleasant and cooperative man, able to converse easily though his daughter adds some details.
Shunt site: Clean, dry, and intact with a confirmed setting of 2.
Cognitive testing: MMSE score of 26 out of 30 when tested with spelling and 25 out of 30 when tested with calculations. Able to get two of the three memory words with cuing, and the third with multiple choice (slight improvement over initial scores).
Gait testing: Tinetti assessment tool tested without an assistive device. Gait score of 6 to 8 out of 12 and balance score of 12 to 16 for a total score of 18 to 20 out of 28 (slightly improved from initial score of 15 to 17).
Cranial nerves: Pupils equal, EOMs intact, face symmetric, no dysarthria.
Motor: Normal for bulk and strength.
Coordination: Slow from finger-to-nose.

RESULTS
Head CT scan from 10/15/2020 shows frontal horn span at the level of foramen of Monro of 4.6 cm with a third ventricular contour that is flat with a span of 10 mm. There is a tiny amount of blood in the right frontal region with a tiny subdermal collection (noted by doctor reading, not noted by radiologist). There is also substantial small vessel ischemic change.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Adult hydrocephalus, gait impairment, urinary incontinence and urgency, and cognitive impairment.
Plan to leave the shunt set at the current level for another 2 to 3 months before changing it, as there are no headaches or pain and he has improved.
Patient to follow up in 3 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left shoulder pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a very active female who presents with left shoulder pain for a few weeks (approximately 3 weeks). She denies any direct or associated trauma, falls, or hitting her shoulder. She has been renovating her basement, which involves doing a lot of activity. She reports that anytime she tries to reach for something or lift anything, she experiences a lot of pain, and she avoids raising her arm over her head due to significant pain. The pain is constant, and pressure—such as trying to sleep on her left side at night—worsens the discomfort. Without Tylenol, her pain level is a 7 out of 10. She takes Extra Strength Tylenol two tablets every 6 to 8 hours, which helps take the edge off and brings her pain down to a 2 or 3 out of 10.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness or tingling in the arm or hand. 
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals reviewed; everything looks good.
Focused exam of the left shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. Tenderness of the greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the sternoclavicular or clavicular joints. Good hand grip bilaterally. Neurovascular exam of the left arm shows brisk capillary refill in less than 3 seconds; motor and sensation are intact to light touch.

RESULTS
X-ray of the left shoulder shows no fracture or bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left shoulder pain, most likely due to rotator cuff tendinopathy.
- Order an MRI of the left shoulder to rule out other pathology.
- Refer for physical therapy for approximately 6 to 8 weeks.
- Continue Tylenol p.r.n. for pain management.
- Discussed possible future consideration of a steroid injection of the left shoulder if symptoms do not improve with conservative treatment.
- Follow up in about two weeks.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old male with a history of hypertension and palpitations. He was recently in the emergency room with high blood pressure and palpitations, which he believes was likely a panic attack related to consuming a few cups of coffee without breakfast on that day; he has not felt it again since. He has had issues with his blood pressure since he was young, with a strong family history of high blood pressure. About a month ago, a new primary care doctor started him on Benicar HCT (a combination medication containing hydrochlorothiazide) and he is also taking amlodipine 10 mg daily. He checks his blood pressure daily every morning upon waking, and it has been running around 146 to 155 lately. He is trying to back off on his salt intake and walks on the treadmill when he can. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart and lungs sound good. Abdomen is soft, non-tender to palpation throughout. Extremities show no ankle or foot swelling.

RESULTS
Potassium level was 4.0 one week ago. Thyroid profile from March 1st, 2021, copied forward.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Resistant hypertension, currently on three medications at maximum doses not yet controlled in the 120s. Add spironolactone to his regimen to help drop aldosterone levels and blood pressure.
2. Discussed potential risks of hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone, including electrolyte balance issues, dehydration (dizziness standing up), elevated potassium (starting potassium is 4.0), lowered sodium levels, dizziness, and rare risk of gynecomastia (chest tenderness or enlarged breasts in men; instruct to discontinue and notify if this occurs).
3. Order repeat basic metabolic panel and blood pressure check in two weeks.
4. Provide information on the DASH eating plan, recommend keeping sodium under 2,000 mg/day (ideal 1,500 mg/day), and suggest visiting heart.org for educational resources on diet, exercise, and blood pressure control.
5. Encourage routine treadmill exercise for 30 minutes most days.
6. If the new medication is ineffective, next steps will include referral to the resistant hypertension clinic to evaluate for secondary causes and discuss potential procedure-based technologies such as renal denervation.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Kidney stone and pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Linda is a female presenting with left back pain starting about three days ago, which she believes is a kidney stone. This is her third time having a kidney stone. The pain is constant, cannot get comfortable, and is traveling a little lower. She has been able to urinate and noticed some blood this morning. She reports chills, not being able to eat due to pain, and feeling a little nauseous, but no fever. She has tried taking Tylenol and ibuprofen, but it is not really working. Past episodes typically resolved in about three to four days. 
She also has a history of hypertension and diabetes. For hypertension, she takes 2.5 mg of Norvasc. She got a blood pressure cuff and reports top numbers usually in the 130s, sometimes 140s, and once 150, with bottom numbers between 70 and 80. She is trying to lower salt intake, though she likes french fries and is open to help with her diet. For diabetes, she takes 500 mg of metformin and checks blood sugars before eating, which are in the low 100s.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever. Reports chills. Denies chest pain. Denies abdominal pain, though back pain is starting to go down into her groin.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally, no crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen: Tenderness to palpation of the abdomen; no rebound or guarding.
Back/Flank: CVA tenderness on the flank.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney stone: Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain. Continue Tylenol for breakthrough pain. Push fluids to help pass the stone. Provide a strainer to strain urine. Refer to urology for evaluation of recurrent kidney stones, even if the stone passes in the next couple of days.
2. Hypertension: Continue Norvasc 2.5 mg. Blood pressures look good; no medication changes made.
3. Diabetes: Continue metformin 500 mg.
4. Diet: Provide referral to nutrition/dietitian for help with diet and reducing salt intake.

Follow-up for chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction and pre-op evaluation for right knee replacement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 74-year-old female with chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction who returns for follow-up. Earlier in the spring, she had a CHF exacerbation with BMP up to 3,000 in March and 6,000 in April. Her diuretic was switched from furosemide to torsemide 20 mg by mouth daily, and her lisinopril was increased to 10 mg daily in March. Symptomatically, she is doing a lot better and has lost about 3 to 3.5 pounds since April. She reports occasional leg cramps which resolve with drinking about 4 ounces of pickle juice. She is scheduled for a right knee replacement on the 24th of June at East Metro. She is also interested in getting an overdue screening colonoscopy done within the next 30 days prior to a potential change in her husband's insurance.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies acute distress; notes weight loss of 3-3.5 pounds.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Had mild leg cramps recently, relieved by pickle juice.
Respiratory: Breathing is non-labored. Denies acute shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Heartburn was bad for a while in January, tried Prilosec and stopped previous medication, no problems since. Using the bathroom okay; oxybutynin is helping with urinary urgency.
Hematologic/Anemia: Denies active bleeding; previously had anemia, iron supplement reviewed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Patient is in no acute distress.
Lungs: Lungs sound pretty good, clear to auscultation, breathing non-labored.
Cardiovascular: Blood pressure is looking good. Heart sounds evaluated.

RESULTS
- Weight: Lost about 3 to 3.5 pounds since April.
- Hemoglobin: Doing great.
- Potassium: 3.9 (holding steady on torsemide).
- Creatinine: 0.7 (appropriate kidney function).
- BUN: 23 (slightly elevated, possible mild dehydration).
- BMP: Pending (was 3,000 in March and 6,000 in April prior to medication change).
- A1C: 5.5 in March (note: provider mentions 5.1 in assessment and plan).
- Blood sugar: 169 today (non-fasting).
- Magnesium: 1.7 (normal range, but provider notes preference for ~2-ish range to stabilize heart muscle).
- Ekg: To be repeated today.
- Chest X-ray: Not needed (done recently).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chronic CHF, mixed presentation: Patient had a CHF exacerbation earlier in the spring. Switched from furosemide to torsemide; symptomatically doing much better, down 3 to 3.5 pounds, breathing non-labored. Continue current regimen. Creatinine is appropriate. Repeat EKG today.
2. Pre-op examination: Right knee replacement scheduled for June 24th at East Metro. Stop clopidogrel one week prior to surgery. Complete a pre-op check within two weeks of surgery (first or second week of June). Repeat EKG today.
3. Colonoscopy: Patient is overdue for a screening colonoscopy. Will attempt to have it performed locally within the next month prior to insurance change. Referral options discussed (County Surgical Services / Dr. Martin at Springfield or Valley Medical). Completing the colonoscopy will not delay the knee surgery.
4. Diabetes: A1c was 5.5 in March (noted as 5.1 in closing assessment). Blood sugar was 169 today (non-fasting); may need repeat pre-op A1c/blood sugar test prior to surgery next month.
5. Supplements: Recommend adding a magnesium supplement (twice daily) to bring level closer to 2-ish to help stabilize heart muscle.

High blood pressure and kidney concerns noted by PCP.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female who presents for evaluation of uncontrolled hypertension and kidney concerns. Her new PCP started seeing her last year and has been adjusting her medications, but her blood pressure remains difficult to control. She feels fine on most days and is busy at work, but can tell when her blood pressure is high, experiencing mild headaches at those times. She denies chest pain and shortness of breath (even with exertion). She reports a small amount of lower extremity swelling if she is on her feet for a long time. 
Diet-wise, she tries to eat better, but during football season she consumes pizza, wings, and subs. She occasionally takes NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve) for knee or back pain, but not every day. Alcohol intake consists of a couple of beers during the week and one or two on the weekends. Family history is positive for high blood pressure in both parents and kidney disease in one parent. Current medications include Norvasc 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice a day; she was previously on lisinopril.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Feels fine most days.
Head: Mild headaches when blood pressure gets really high.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No shortness of breath, even with exertion.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Diet includes pizza, wings, and subs during football season.
Musculoskeletal: Occasional knee and back pain; mild lower extremity swelling if on feet for a long time.
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted.

Vitals: Blood pressure 169/74, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98%.
Neck: No jugular vein distention, no carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, 2/6 systolic ejection murmur with an extra sound heard.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

Assessment: Uncontrolled hypertension, likely multifactorial.

7. Keep a record of home blood pressures taken at the same time every day and bring the log to the next visit.
8. Return to the office in 3 weeks.
9. Doctor will coordinate care and communicate plans with the patient's PCP.
